\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The objects}

Dedekind's eta function is the infinite product
\[
  \eta(\tau)=q^{1/24}\prod_{n\ge1}(1-q^n),\qquad q=e^{2\pi i\tau},\ \Im\tau>0 .
\]
An \emph{eta quotient} is a finite product of rescaled eta functions with
integer exponents,
\[
  \eta_a(\tau)=\prod_{k\ge1}\eta(k\tau)^{a_k},
\]
with $a:\N\to\Z$ finitely supported. Eta quotients are the most explicitly
computable family of modular forms: they include the modular discriminant
$\Delta=\eta^{24}$, the partition generating function, and weight-two newforms
of small level.

Collecting fractional $q$-powers, the leading behaviour of $\eta_a$ is
$q^{w(a)/24}$ with $w(a)=\sum_k k\,a_k$. Call $a$ \emph{admissible} when
$w(a)=24$; then the leading term is exactly $q$, all fractional exponents
cancel, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:regroup}
  \eta_a(\tau)=q\prod_{m\ge1}(1-q^m)^{b_m},\qquad b_m=\sum_{k\mid m}a_k .
\end{equation}
The regrouping \eqref{eq:regroup} --- the factor $\eta(k\tau)$ contributes
$(1-q^{kn})$ for every $n\ge1$, so that $(1-q^m)$ collects $a_k$ over all
divisors $k$ of $m$ --- turns the arithmetic of eta quotients into the
arithmetic of divisor sums.

Inverting and clearing the pole yields the central object:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:F}
  F_a(q):=\frac{q}{\eta_a}=\prod_{m\ge1}(1-q^m)^{-b_m}=\sum_{n\ge0}A_nq^n
  \ \in\ \Z[\![q]\!]^\times ,
\end{equation}
related to the \emph{Hauptmodul normal form}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normal}
  \frac{1}{\eta_a}=q^{-1}+c(0)+c(1)q+c(2)q^2+\cdots
\end{equation}
by $A_n=c(n-1)$. We call $c(1)=A_2$ the \emph{head coefficient} of $a$ and
write $\hc(a)$; it is the first coefficient not forced by the normalisation.

\subsection{Main results}

Throughout, $F_a^{(N)}=\prod_{m=1}^{N}(1-q^m)^{-b_m}$ is the truncated product,
a unit of $\Z[\![q]\!]$.

\begin{theoremletter}[Head coefficient]\label{thm:A}
For every finitely supported $a:\N\to\Z$ and every $N\ge2$, the coefficient of
$q^2$ in $F_a^{(N)}$ equals
\[
  \hc(a)=\frac{a_1(a_1+3)}{2}+a_2 ,
\]
independently of $N$. Moreover the coefficient of $q$ is $a_1$ and the constant
coefficient is $1$; in the normal form \eqref{eq:normal}, $c(-1)=1$,
$c(0)=a_1$, $c(1)=\hc(a)$.
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Second coefficient]\label{thm:B}
For every $N\ge3$, the coefficient of $q^3$ in $F_a^{(N)}$ is
\[
  c(2)=\frac{a_1(a_1+1)(a_1+2)}{6}+a_1(a_1+a_2)+a_1+a_3 .
\]
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Stability]\label{thm:C}
If $n\le N$ and $n\le M$, the coefficient of $q^n$ in $F_a^{(N)}$ equals that in
$F_a^{(M)}$. Hence $A_n$ is well defined by any truncation of length at least
$n$, and Theorems \ref{thm:A} and \ref{thm:B} are statements about the infinite
product \eqref{eq:F}.
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Heisenberg cocycle and matrix bridge]\label{thm:D}
$F_{a+a'}=F_aF_{a'}$ and
\[
  \hc(a+a')=\hc(a)+\hc(a')+a_1a_1' .
\]
The assignment
$M(a)=\begin{pmatrix}1&a_1&\hc(a)\\0&1&a_1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$
satisfies $M(a+a')=M(a)M(a')$ and $\det M(a)=1$: it is a homomorphism from the
additive group of exponent vectors to the discrete Heisenberg group
$H_3(\Z)\le\mathrm{SL}_3(\Z)$.
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Recursion in all degrees]\label{thm:E}
Let $\sigma_b(j)=\sum_{m\mid j,\,m\le N}m\,b_m$. Then $A_0=1$ and, for all
$n\ge1$,
\[
  n\,A_n=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}A_i\,\sigma_b(n-i).
\]
The structure constants are additive in $a$, and for $j\le N$ the quantity
$\sigma_b(j)$ is the full divisor sum $\sum_{m\mid j}m\,b_m$, independent of
the truncation.
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Positivity]\label{thm:F}
If $b_m\ge0$ for $1\le m\le N$ then $A_n\ge0$ for all $n$; if moreover
$b_1\ge1$ then $A_n\ge1$ for all $n$. In particular every coefficient of
$q/\Delta=\prod_m(1-q^m)^{-24}$, namely $1,24,324,3200,25650,176256,\dots$, is
at least $1$.
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Congruence]\label{thm:G}
If $d\mid b_m$ for $1\le m\le N$ then $d\mid n\,A_n$ for all $n\ge1$; if
moreover $\gcd(d,n)=1$ then $d\mid A_n$. For $q/\Delta$: $24\mid A_n$ whenever
$\gcd(n,24)=1$, and then $A_n\ge24$. The coprimality hypothesis is not
removable, since $A_2=324$ and $24\nmid324$.
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Arithmetic of the head coefficient]\label{thm:H}
For pure exponent vectors ($a_2=0$), an integer $c$ is a head coefficient if and
only if $8c+9$ is a perfect square; $c=1$ is not attained; $c\ge-1$ always,
with equality exactly at $a_1\in\{-1,-2\}$; and the value is unchanged exactly
under $a_1\mapsto-3-a_1$. Allowing $a_2\ne0$, every integer $c$ is the head
coefficient of an admissible exponent vector, e.g.\
$a_2=c$, $a_3=2c-24$, $a_4=24-2c$.
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Tropical layer and its incompleteness]\label{thm:I}
The tropicalised $q$-adic order $T(f)=\trop(\ord f)$ satisfies
$T(fg)=T(f)\otimes T(g)$ and $T(f)\oplus T(g)\le T(f+g)$. For every $a$ and
every $N\ge2$, $T(F_a^{(N)})$ is the tropical unit; consequently $T$ cannot
distinguish exponent vectors whose head coefficients differ by $324$.
\end{theoremletter}

\section{Jet calculus and the head coefficient}

\subsection{Two-jets}

Work in $\Z[\![X]\!]$ and write $[X^n]f$ for the coefficient of $X^n$.

\begin{definition}
For $f\in\Z[\![X]\!]$ and $c_1,c_2\in\Z$, say $f$ has \emph{jet} $(c_1,c_2)$,
written $J(f)=(c_1,c_2)$, if $[X^0]f=1$, $[X^1]f=c_1$, $[X^2]f=c_2$, i.e.\
$f=1+c_1X+c_2X^2+O(X^3)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Jet group law]\label{lem:jetmul}
If $J(f)=(c_1,c_2)$ and $J(g)=(d_1,d_2)$ then
$J(fg)=(c_1+d_1,\ c_2+c_1d_1+d_2)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Convolution: $[X^1](fg)=[X^0]f\,[X^1]g+[X^1]f\,[X^0]g$ and
$[X^2](fg)=[X^0]f\,[X^2]g+[X^1]f\,[X^1]g+[X^2]f\,[X^0]g$; substitute.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Inversion]\label{lem:jetinv}
If $u$ is a unit with $J(u)=(c_1,c_2)$ then $J(u^{-1})=(-c_1,\ c_1^2-c_2)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma \ref{lem:jetmul} to $uu^{-1}=1$, whose jet is $(0,0)$, and solve
degree by degree.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Integer powers]\label{lem:jetpow}
If $J(u)=(c_1,c_2)$ then for every $n\in\Z$,
\[
  J(u^n)=\Bigl(nc_1,\ nc_2+\binom{n}{2}c_1^2\Bigr),\qquad
  \binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2},
\]
the triangular number extended to all integers.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induct in both directions from $n=0$: the step $n\to n+1$ uses Lemma
\ref{lem:jetmul} and $\binom{n+1}{2}=\binom{n}{2}+n$; the step $n\to n-1$ uses
Lemma \ref{lem:jetinv} and $\binom{n-1}{2}=\binom{n}{2}-(n-1)$.
\end{proof}

Lemma \ref{lem:jetpow} is the engine: the appearance of $\binom{n}{2}$ is the
degree-two truncation of $\exp(n\log u)$, and it is the source of the quadratic
term in Theorem \ref{thm:A}. Two consequences of Lemma \ref{lem:jetmul} are
used repeatedly: a product of series with jet $(0,0)$ has jet $(0,0)$, and
multiplying by a series with jet $(0,0)$ preserves jets.

\subsection{The basic factors}

For $m\ge1$ the series $1-X^m$ is a unit, and
\[
  J(1-X)=(-1,0),\qquad J(1-X^2)=(0,-1),\qquad J(1-X^m)=(0,0)\ (m\ge3),
\]
since $1-X^m$ differs from $1$ only in degree $m$.

\subsection{Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:A}}

Set $b_m=\sum_{k\mid m}a_k$; in particular $b_1=a_1$, $b_2=a_1+a_2$. Induct on
$N\ge2$.

\emph{Base $N=2$.} By Lemma \ref{lem:jetpow},
$J\bigl((1-X)^{-b_1}\bigr)=\bigl(b_1,\binom{-b_1}{2}\bigr)
=\bigl(a_1,\tfrac{a_1(a_1+1)}{2}\bigr)$, using $\binom{-b}{2}=\tfrac{b(b+1)}{2}$,
and $J\bigl((1-X^2)^{-b_2}\bigr)=(0,b_2)=(0,a_1+a_2)$. Lemma \ref{lem:jetmul}
gives
\[
  J\bigl(F^{(2)}\bigr)
  =\Bigl(a_1,\ \tfrac{a_1(a_1+1)}{2}+a_1\cdot0+a_1+a_2\Bigr)
  =\Bigl(a_1,\ \tfrac{a_1(a_1+3)}{2}+a_2\Bigr).
\]

\emph{Step.} For $N\ge2$ the new factor $(1-X^{N+1})^{-b_{N+1}}$ has jet $(0,0)$
by Lemma \ref{lem:jetpow} applied to $J(1-X^{N+1})=(0,0)$, so multiplying by it
leaves the jet unchanged. \qed

The head coefficient is thus a sum of two contributions of different natures: a
quadratic one from the single factor $(1-X)^{-b_1}$ and a linear one from
$(1-X^2)^{-b_2}$. For $a=24\delta_1$ (that is, $\Delta=\eta^{24}$, admissible
since $1\cdot24=24$) we get $\hc=24\cdot27/2=324$; for $a=12\delta_2$
(that is, $\eta(2\tau)^{12}$, admissible since $2\cdot12=24$) we get $\hc=12$.

\subsection{Three-jets and Theorem \ref{thm:B}}

Recording $[X^3]f=c_3$ as well, the power law becomes
\[
  J_3(u^n)=\Bigl(nc_1,\ nc_2+\binom{n}{2}c_1^2,\
  nc_3+n(n-1)c_1c_2+\binom{n}{3}c_1^3\Bigr),
\]
with $\binom{n}{3}=\tfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}$ the tetrahedral number extended to
$\Z$. Running the same induction with
$J_3(1-X)=(-1,0,0)$, $J_3(1-X^2)=(0,-1,0)$, $J_3(1-X^3)=(0,0,-1)$,
$J_3(1-X^m)=(0,0,0)$ for $m\ge4$, and $b_3=a_1+a_3$, together with the identity
$-\binom{-b}{3}=\tfrac{b(b+1)(b+2)}{6}$, yields Theorem \ref{thm:B}. For
$a=24\delta_1$ the formula returns $2600+576+24=3200$, matching
$1/\Delta=q^{-1}+24+324q+3200q^2+\cdots$. The pattern suggests that in degree
$n$ the coefficient $c(n-1)$ is a polynomial of weighted degree $n$ in
$a_1,\dots,a_n$ for $\wt(a_k)=k$, with top part $\pm\binom{-a_1}{n}$ and bottom
part the linear term $a_n$.

\section{Stability of the truncation}

\begin{definition}
For $k\ge0$ write $f\equiv1\pmod{X^k}$ when $X^k\mid f-1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:onemod}
This relation is stable under products, under inversion of units, under integer
powers of units, and it weakens when $k$ decreases.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$fg-1=(f-1)g+(g-1)$; $u^{-1}-1=u^{-1}(1-u)$; integer powers follow by induction;
weakening is $X^k\mid X^l$ for $k\le l$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:tail}
$1-X^m\equiv1\pmod{X^m}$, and if $g\equiv1\pmod{X^k}$ then $[X^n](fg)=[X^n]f$
for all $n<k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The first is immediate; for the second, $fg-f=f(g-1)$ is divisible by $X^k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:C}]
For $N\le M$, write $F^{(M)}=F^{(N)}\prod_{m=N+1}^{M}(1-X^m)^{-b_m}$. By Lemmas
\ref{lem:onemod} and \ref{lem:tail} the tail is $\equiv1\pmod{X^{N+1}}$, so
coefficients agree in all degrees $\le N$. For general $N,M\ge n$ compare both
to $F^{(\max(N,M))}$.
\end{proof}

Consequently $A_n:=[X^n]F^{(n)}$ is well defined, computed by any truncation of
length $\ge n$, and $A_0=1$, $A_1=a_1$, $A_2=\hc(a)$ hold for the infinite
product.

\subsection{Divisor regrouping in low degree}

Let $P_a^{(N)}=\prod_{k=1}^{N}\bigl(\prod_{n=1}^{N}(1-X^{kn})\bigr)^{a_k}$ be
the truncated eta product without $q$-normalisation and
$D_a^{(N)}=\prod_{m=1}^{N}(1-X^m)^{b_m}$ its divisor-sum form.

\begin{proposition}
For $N\ge2$,
\[
  J\bigl(P_a^{(N)}\bigr)=J\bigl(D_a^{(N)}\bigr)
  =\Bigl(-a_1,\ \tfrac{a_1(a_1-1)}{2}-a_1-a_2\Bigr),
\]
and consequently $J\bigl(P_a^{(N)}F_a^{(N)}\bigr)=(0,0)$: the identity
$(\eta_a/q)\cdot(q/\eta_a)=1$ holds to the accuracy at which the head
coefficient is computed.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For $P$: the $k=1$ factor $\prod_n(1-X^n)$ has jet $(-1,-1)$ and is raised to
$a_1$; the $k=2$ factor $\prod_n(1-X^{2n})$ has jet $(0,-1)$ and is raised to
$a_2$; factors with $k\ge3$ have jet $(0,0)$. For $D$: use $b_1=a_1$,
$b_2=a_1+a_2$ and the jets of the basic factors. Both computations give the
displayed pair; the last claim follows from Lemma \ref{lem:jetmul} and Theorem
\ref{thm:A}.
\end{proof}

\section{The Heisenberg cocycle}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:mult}
$b_\bullet$ is additive in $a$, hence $F^{(N)}_{a+a'}=F^{(N)}_aF^{(N)}_{a'}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$b_m(a+a')=\sum_{k\mid m}(a_k+a_k')=b_m(a)+b_m(a')$, and
$(1-X^m)^{-(b+b')}=(1-X^m)^{-b}(1-X^m)^{-b'}$ factorwise.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:D}]
Multiplicativity is Proposition \ref{prop:mult}. For the cocycle, apply Theorem
\ref{thm:A} three times:
\[
  \frac{(a_1+a_1')(a_1+a_1'+3)}{2}+(a_2+a_2')
  =\frac{a_1(a_1+3)}{2}+a_2+\frac{a_1'(a_1'+3)}{2}+a_2'+a_1a_1',
\]
all divisions being exact because $n(n+3)$ is even. Equivalently this is Lemma
\ref{lem:jetmul} in degree $2$: the cross-term $c_1d_1$ \emph{is} the cocycle.
For the matrices,
\[
  \begin{pmatrix}1&a_1&h\\0&1&a_1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}
  \begin{pmatrix}1&a_1'&h'\\0&1&a_1'\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}
  =\begin{pmatrix}1&a_1+a_1'&h+h'+a_1a_1'\\0&1&a_1+a_1'\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},
\]
which equals $M(a+a')$ precisely by the cocycle identity; the determinant of a
unipotent upper-triangular matrix is $1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The invariants $c(0)=a_1$ and $c(1)=\hc(a)$ form a two-step tower: the first is
a homomorphism to $(\Z,+)$, the second only modulo the commutator, with
obstruction the symmetric form $(a,a')\mapsto a_1a_1'$. The head coefficient
lives in the centre of $H_3(\Z)$. This is the smallest non-abelian phenomenon a
$q$-expansion can exhibit, and eta quotients realise it explicitly.
\end{remark}

\section{The logarithmic-derivative recursion}

Jet calculus is degree-by-degree; this section replaces it with one uniform
statement.

\subsection{The Euler operator}

Write $D=\frac{d}{dX}$ and, for a unit $u$,
\[
  L(u):=X\frac{Du}{u}=X\,(Du)\,u^{-1},
\]
the Euler operator $q\frac{d}{dq}$ applied to $\log u$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:L}
$L(1)=0$, $L(uv)=L(u)+L(v)$, $L(u^{-1})=-L(u)$, $L(u^n)=nL(u)$ for $n\in\Z$,
and $L(\prod_iu_i)=\sum_iL(u_i)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The product rule $D(uv)=u\,Dv+v\,Du$ divided by $uv$; the rest is formal.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:Lfactor}
For $m\ge1$, $L(1-X^m)=-m\dfrac{X^m}{1-X^m}$, and
$\dfrac{X^m}{1-X^m}=\sum_{j\ge1}[m\mid j]X^j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$D(1-X^m)=-mX^{m-1}$; the geometric expansion
$(1-X^m)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}X^{mk}$ is verified by multiplying out.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:logD}
With $F=F_a^{(N)}$,
\[
  L(F)=\sum_{m=1}^{N}m\,b_m\frac{X^m}{1-X^m},\qquad
  [X^j]L(F)=\sigma_b(j):=\sum_{\substack{m\mid j\\ m\le N}}m\,b_m\ (j\ge1),
\]
and $[X^0]L(F)=0$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Lemma \ref{lem:L} turns the product into $\sum_m -b_m L(1-X^m)$ and Lemma
\ref{lem:Lfactor} evaluates each term; the $j$-th coefficient selects the
divisors of $j$.
\end{proof}

The quantity $\sigma_b(j)$ is a \emph{twisted divisor sum}: for $b\equiv1$ it is
the classical $\sigma_1(j)$, and for $q/\Delta$ it is $24\sigma_1(j)$.

\subsection{Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:E}}

Multiplying the definition of $L$ by $F$ gives $F\cdot L(F)=X\,DF$. Take the
coefficient of $X^n$, $n\ge1$. On the right, $[X^n](X\,DF)=[X^{n-1}]DF=nA_n$; on
the left, convolution gives $\sum_{i=0}^{n}A_i[X^{n-i}]L(F)$, whose $i=n$ term
vanishes since $[X^0]L(F)=0$, the rest being $A_i\sigma_b(n-i)$ by Proposition
\ref{prop:logD}. Finally $A_0=1$ because the constant-term map is a ring
homomorphism and each factor has constant term $1$. Additivity of $\sigma_b$ in
$a$ is inherited from that of $b$; for $j\le N$ every divisor $m$ of $j$
satisfies $m\le N$, so the truncation removes nothing. \qed

\subsection{An independent derivation of Theorem \ref{thm:A}}

One computes $\sigma_b(1)=b_1=a_1$ and $\sigma_b(2)=b_1+2b_2=3a_1+2a_2$. Then
$n=1$ gives $A_1=A_0\sigma_b(1)=a_1$, and $n=2$ gives
\[
  2A_2=A_0\sigma_b(2)+A_1\sigma_b(1)=(3a_1+2a_2)+a_1^2,
  \qquad A_2=\frac{a_1(a_1+3)}{2}+a_2 .
\]
This derivation shares no lemma with the jet calculus, so the two together are
an independent double check of the head-coefficient formula.

\section{Positivity and congruences}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sigpos}
If $b_m\ge0$ for $1\le m\le N$ then $\sigma_b(j)\ge0$ for all $j$; and since
$m=1$ divides every $j$, $\sigma_b(j)\ge b_1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Each summand $m\,b_m$ is a product of nonnegatives; isolating the $m=1$ term
leaves a nonnegative remainder.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:F}]
Strong induction. $A_0=1$. For $n\ge1$, $nA_n=\sum_{i<n}A_i\sigma_b(n-i)$ is a
sum of products of nonnegatives by induction and Lemma \ref{lem:sigpos}, so
$A_n\ge0$. If moreover $b_1\ge1$, each of the $n$ summands is $\ge1$, so
$nA_n\ge n$ and $A_n\ge1$. For $q/\Delta$, $a=24\delta_1$ gives $b_m=24$ for
every $m\ge1$, so both hypotheses hold.
\end{proof}

Observe the role of the divisor regrouping: the exponent vector of $\Delta$ is
supported at a single index, but the divisor data $b$ is the constant sequence
$24$. Positivity is a statement about $b$, not $a$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sigdvd}
If $d\mid b_m$ for $1\le m\le N$ then $d\mid\sigma_b(j)$ for all $j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Each summand $m\,b_m$ is divisible by $d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:G}]
By Theorem \ref{thm:E}, $nA_n=\sum_{i<n}A_i\sigma_b(n-i)$, and every summand is
divisible by $d$ by Lemma \ref{lem:sigdvd}; hence $d\mid nA_n$, and if
$\gcd(d,n)=1$ then $d\mid A_n$. For $q/\Delta$ take $d=24$. The sequence begins
\[
  A_0,\dots,A_7=1,\ 24,\ 324,\ 3200,\ 25650,\ 176256,\ 1073720,\ 5930496,
\]
and $24\mid24$, $24\mid176256=24\cdot7344$, $24\mid5930496=24\cdot247104$ at the
indices $1,5,7$ coprime to $24$, whereas $324,3200,25650$ at indices $2,3,4$ are
not divisible by $24$: the coprimality hypothesis is not removable.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
For $q/\Delta$ and every $n\ge1$ with $\gcd(n,24)=1$, the coefficient $A_n$ is a
positive multiple of $24$, hence $A_n\ge24$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorems \ref{thm:F} and \ref{thm:G}: $A_n=24t$ with $A_n\ge1$ forces
$t\ge1$.
\end{proof}

The mechanism is general: any eta quotient whose divisor data share a common
factor $d$ inherits $d\mid A_n$ for every $n$ coprime to $d$ --- a divisibility
phenomenon of moonshine flavour obtained with no modular input, only the
recursion.

\section{Which integers are head coefficients?}

Restrict first to pure vectors, $a_2=0$, so $\hc(a)=\tfrac{n(n+3)}{2}$ with
$n=a_1$; the values for $n=-4,\dots,4$ are $2,0,-1,-1,0,2,5,9,14$.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:dioph}
An integer $c$ satisfies $c=\tfrac{n(n+3)}{2}$ for some $n\in\Z$ if and only if
$8c+9$ is a perfect square.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If $2c=n(n+3)$ then $8c+9=(2n+3)^2$. Conversely if $s^2=8c+9$ then $s$ is odd,
say $s=2u+1$, and $(u-1)(u+2)=2c$, so $n=u-1$ works.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$c=1$ is not a pure head coefficient, since $17$ is not a square.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proposition}
$\tfrac{n(n+3)}{2}=\tfrac{n'(n'+3)}{2}$ if and only if $n'=n$ or $n'=-3-n$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Clearing denominators, $(n-n')(n+n'+3)=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Integrality rigidity]
$\tfrac{n(n+3)}{2}\ge-1$ for all $n\in\Z$, with equality exactly at $n=-1,-2$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$(n+1)(n+2)\ge0$ for consecutive integers, so $n(n+3)=(n+1)(n+2)-2\ge-2$, with
equality iff $(n+1)(n+2)=0$.
\end{proof}

The real quadratic $x(x+3)/2$ attains $-9/8$ at $x=-3/2$; the integer minimum
$-1$ is strictly larger.

\begin{theorem}[Surjectivity on admissible vectors]
For every $c\in\Z$ there is a finitely supported $a$ with $\sum_kka_k=24$ and
$\hc(a)=c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $a_2=c$, $a_3=2c-24$, $a_4=24-2c$ and all other $a_k=0$. Then
$\sum_kka_k=2c+6c-72+96-8c=24$ and, as $a_1=0$, $\hc(a)=a_2=c$.
\end{proof}

So the arithmetic obstruction of Proposition \ref{prop:dioph} is a feature of
the slice $a_2=0$ only: the second exponent is a free additive dial. Concretely
$c=1$, unattainable by pure powers, is attained by $a=(0,1,-22,22,0,\dots)$.

\section{The tropical layer}

The tropical semiring on $\N\cup\{\infty\}$ has $x\otimes y=x+y$ and
$x\oplus y=\min(x,y)$. The $X$-adic order $\ord(f)$ is a valuation and becomes
semiring-compatible after tropicalisation; write $T(f)=\trop(\ord f)$.

\begin{proposition}
$T(fg)=T(f)\otimes T(g)$; $T(f)\oplus T(g)\le T(f+g)$; $T(1)$ is the tropical
unit, $T(0)$ the tropical zero, $T(X^n)=\trop(n)$, and
$T(f^n)=T(f)^{\otimes n}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
These are $\ord(fg)=\ord f+\ord g$ (valid since $\Z[\![X]\!]$ is a domain) and
$\ord(f+g)\ge\min(\ord f,\ord g)$, restated tropically.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:tropunit}
For every $a$ and $N\ge2$, $\ord(F_a^{(N)})=0$ and $T(F_a^{(N)})$ is the
tropical unit; hence $a\mapsto T(F_a^{(N)})$ is a constant monoid homomorphism.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$F_a^{(N)}$ is a unit with constant term $1$ by Theorem \ref{thm:A}, so its
order is $0$; multiplicativity is Proposition \ref{prop:mult}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:I}]
Take $a=24\delta_1$ and $a'=0$: both have tropically trivial shadow by
Proposition \ref{prop:tropunit}, while $\hc(a)=324$ and $\hc(a')=0$.
\end{proof}

The content is the strictness. The normalisation $F_a=q/\eta_a$ pushes all
$q$-adic valuation into the explicit factor $q$; the tropical layer is the
trivial, abelianised bottom of an invariant tower whose next floor --- the head
coefficient --- is Heisenberg and non-abelian.

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithmx}[Head coefficient in $O(1)$]
Given $a_1,a_2$, return $a_1(a_1+3)/2+a_2$. Two multiplications, one shift, one
addition; exact in integer arithmetic since $n(n+3)$ is always even. The naive
alternative expands the product and needs $\Theta(N)$ series multiplications.
\end{algorithmx}

\begin{algorithmx}[All coefficients by the recursion, $O(n^2+n\log n)$]
Sieve $b_m=\sum_{k\mid m}a_k$ for $m\le n$ over multiples ($O(n\log n)$), sieve
$\sigma_b(j)=\sum_{m\mid j}m\,b_m$ likewise, then iterate $A_0=1$ and
$nA_n=\sum_{i<n}A_i\sigma_b(n-i)$. The convolution dominates at $O(n^2)$
integer multiplications; every division is exact, so the computation stays in
$\Z$.
\end{algorithmx}

\begin{algorithmx}[Direct product expansion, used as a cross-check]
Multiply the truncated factors $(1-q^m)^{-b_m}$ one at a time using
$(1-q^m)^{-b}=\sum_{j\ge0}\binom{b+j-1}{j}q^{mj}$ for $b\ge0$ and the finite
binomial expansion for $b<0$. Stability (Theorem \ref{thm:C}) guarantees
termination at $m=n$ with the correct answer.
\end{algorithmx}

\section{Discussion and future directions}

\subsection{Why the head coefficient is the right invariant}

In the normal form $1/\eta_a=q^{-1}+c(0)+c(1)q+\cdots$, the leading $q^{-1}$ is
forced by admissibility and $c(0)=a_1$ is linear. The head coefficient is the
first invariant carrying non-linear information, and Theorem \ref{thm:D}
identifies its nature: it is the central coordinate of a Heisenberg-valued
homomorphism. Genus-zero Hauptmoduln and McKay--Thompson series are written in
exactly this normal form, and several of them are eta quotients; Theorem
\ref{thm:A} gives their head coefficients with no expansion at all.

\subsection{The role of the recursion}

Theorem \ref{thm:E} is the structural centre: pass to the logarithmic
derivative, where $a\mapsto\log F_a$ is exactly linear, and all non-linearity of
the coefficients becomes the non-linearity of $\exp$. Unipotent groups are the
truncations of $\exp$, which is why they govern the coefficient tower; the
Heisenberg cocycle is the degree-two shadow of a Baker--Campbell--Hausdorff
expansion. It also explains why positivity and congruences are cheap once the
recursion is available: both are inherited from the structure constants and
propagated by an induction that never leaves $\Z$.

\subsection{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Unipotent tower]
For each $n\ge1$ let $\Phi_n(a)=(c(0),\dots,c(n-1))\in\Z^n$. Then $\Phi_n$ is a
group homomorphism from the additive group of exponent vectors into a unipotent
group $U_n\le\mathrm{GL}_{n+1}(\Z)$ of upper-triangular matrices with $1$s on
the diagonal, extending $M(a)$, and the $k$-th layer of the lower central series
of the image is generated by the degree-$k$ part of $c(k-1)$ as a polynomial in
$a_1,\dots,a_k$. Concretely, $c(n-1)$ minus its term linear in $a_n$ is a
polynomial in $a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$ of weighted degree exactly $n$ for
$\wt(a_k)=k$. The conjecture reduces to a purely combinatorial statement about
the recursion and is falsifiable at $n=4$ by a finite computation.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Sharp congruence]
Let $d=\gcd\{b_m:m\ge1\}$. Then $c(n-1)\equiv0\pmod{d/\gcd(d,n)}$ for every
$n\ge1$, and this is sharp: for each $n$ there is an admissible $a$ for which
$d/\gcd(d,n)$ is exactly the largest modulus dividing $c(n-1)$.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Positivity is exactly nonnegativity of the divisor data]
All coefficients $c(n-1)$ are positive if and only if $b_m\ge0$ for all $m$ and
$b_1\ge1$; that is, a single negative $b_m$ eventually forces a negative
coefficient.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Weighted-degree growth]
For fixed $n$ and large $a_1$, the polynomial expressing $c(n-1)$ in
$a_1,\dots,a_n$ has leading term $a_1^n/n!$, so
$c(n-1)=\tfrac{a_1^n}{n!}\bigl(1+O(1/a_1)\bigr)$.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Independence of the invariant layers]
The tropical layer, the abelian layer $c(0)=a_1$, and the Heisenberg layer
$c(1)$ are pairwise independent on admissible exponent vectors: any values of
the latter two consistent with the Diophantine constraints above are realised
simultaneously by some admissible $a$.
\end{conjecture}

\section{Summary}

For an eta quotient $\eta_a=\prod_k\eta(k\tau)^{a_k}$ with $\sum_kka_k=24$,
normalised to $F_a=q/\eta_a=\prod_m(1-q^m)^{-b_m}$ with $b_m=\sum_{k\mid m}a_k$,
the head coefficient of the Hauptmodul-shaped expansion is
\[
  c(1)=\frac{a_1(a_1+3)}{2}+a_2,
\]
alongside $c(0)=a_1$ and
$c(2)=\tfrac16a_1(a_1+1)(a_1+2)+a_1(a_1+a_2)+a_1+a_3$. These values are
independent of any truncation; the head coefficient satisfies the Heisenberg
cocycle and defines a homomorphism to $H_3(\Z)$; and all coefficients obey the
recursion $nA_n=\sum_{i<n}A_i\sigma_b(n-i)$ with twisted divisor-sum structure
constants, from which follow positivity of the coefficient sequence of
$q/\Delta$ and the congruence $24\mid A_n$ for $\gcd(n,24)=1$. The attainable
head coefficients are exactly those with $8c+9$ a square in the pure case and
all of $\Z$ in general, and the tropical valuation layer is strictly coarser
than the head coefficient.

so the normalised quotient

    F_a(q) = q / eta_a = prod_m (1 - q^m)^{-b_m} = sum_{n >= 0} A_n q^n

has A_0 = 1, and in the Hauptmodul normal form 1/eta_a = q^{-1} + c(0) + c(1) q + ...
one has c(n-1) = A_n.

Results demonstrated
--------------------
1.  Head coefficient       c(1) = a_1 (a_1 + 3) / 2 + a_2
2.  Constant term          c(0) = a_1
3.  Second coefficient     c(2) = a_1(a_1+1)(a_1+2)/6 + a_1(a_1+a_2) + a_1 + a_3
4.  Stability              [q^n] F^{(N)} independent of the truncation N >= n
5.  Heisenberg cocycle     c(1)(a+a') = c(1)(a) + c(1)(a') + a_1 a'_1
    and the matrix bridge  M(a + a') = M(a) M(a') into the Heisenberg group
6.  Recursion              n A_n = sum_{i<n} A_i sigma_b(n-i),  sigma_b(j) = sum_{m|j} m b_m
7.  Positivity             b >= 0 and b_1 >= 1  =>  A_n >= 1  for all n
8.  Congruence             d | b_m for all m and gcd(d,n) = 1  =>  d | A_n
                           (for 1/Delta: 24 | A_n whenever gcd(n,24) = 1, and
                            A_2 = 324 shows the coprimality cannot be dropped)

from __future__ import annotations

from math import comb, gcd, isqrt
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

Vector = Dict[int, int]  # sparse exponent vector a : index k -> a_k (k >= 1)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic data attached to an exponent vector
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def a_of(a: Vector, k: int) -> int:
    """The exponent a_k (zero outside the support)."""
    return a.get(k, 0)


def weight(a: Vector) -> int:
    """The admissibility weight  sum_k k * a_k  (equals 24 for admissible vectors)."""
    return sum(k * v for k, v in a.items())


def b_coeff(a: Vector, m: int) -> int:
    """Divisor data  b_m = sum_{k | m} a_k."""
    return sum(a_of(a, k) for k in range(1, m + 1) if m % k == 0)


def b_vector(a: Vector, n: int) -> List[int]:
    """[b_0 (unused), b_1, ..., b_n], computed by a sieve over multiples: O(n log n)."""
    b = [0] * (n + 1)
    for k, v in a.items():
        if v == 0 or k < 1:
            continue
        for m in range(k, n + 1, k):
            b[m] += v
    return b


def sigma_b(a: Vector, j: int) -> int:
    """Twisted divisor sum  sigma_b(j) = sum_{m | j} m * b_m."""
    return sum(m * b_coeff(a, m) for m in range(1, j + 1) if j % m == 0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Closed forms proved in the paper
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def head_coeff(a: Vector) -> int:
    """c(1) = a_1 (a_1 + 3) / 2 + a_2.  Exact: n(n+3) is always even."""
    a1, a2 = a_of(a, 1), a_of(a, 2)
    return (a1 * (a1 + 3)) // 2 + a2


def constant_coeff(a: Vector) -> int:
    """c(0) = a_1."""
    return a_of(a, 1)


def second_coeff(a: Vector) -> int:
    """c(2) = a_1(a_1+1)(a_1+2)/6 + a_1(a_1 + a_2) + a_1 + a_3."""
    a1, a2, a3 = a_of(a, 1), a_of(a, 2), a_of(a, 3)
    return (a1 * (a1 + 1) * (a1 + 2)) // 6 + a1 * (a1 + a2) + a1 + a3


def head_matrix(a: Vector) -> Tuple[Tuple[int, int, int], ...]:
    """The unipotent 3x3 matrix M(a) = [[1, a_1, c(1)], [0, 1, a_1], [0, 0, 1]]."""
    a1, h = a_of(a, 1), head_coeff(a)
    return ((1, a1, h), (0, 1, a1), (0, 0, 1))


def mat_mul(
    x: Tuple[Tuple[int, int, int], ...], y: Tuple[Tuple[int, int, int], ...]
) -> Tuple[Tuple[int, int, int], ...]:
    """Ordinary 3x3 integer matrix product."""
    return tuple(
        tuple(sum(x[i][k] * y[k][j] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)
    )


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two independent coefficient engines
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def coeffs_by_product(a: Vector, n_max: int, trunc: int | None = None) -> List[int]:
    """
    Coefficients A_0, ..., A_{n_max} of the truncated product
    F^{(N)} = prod_{m=1}^{N} (1 - q^m)^{-b_m}, expanded factor by factor.

    Uses (1-q^m)^{-b} = sum_j C(b+j-1, j) q^{mj} for b >= 0 and the finite
    binomial expansion (1-q^m)^{|b|} for b < 0.  Complexity O(N * n_max) terms.
    """
    n = n_max
    N = n if trunc is None else trunc
    b = b_vector(a, max(N, n))
    poly = [0] * (n + 1)
    poly[0] = 1
    for m in range(1, N + 1):
        e = b[m] if m < len(b) else 0
        if e == 0:
            continue
        # coefficients of (1 - q^m)^{-e} up to degree n, as a list indexed by j
        factor: List[int] = [0] * (n + 1)
        j = 0
        while m * j <= n:
            if e > 0:
                factor[m * j] = comb(e + j - 1, j)
            else:
                factor[m * j] = (-1) ** j * comb(-e, j) if j <= -e else 0
            j += 1
        out = [0] * (n + 1)
        for i, ci in enumerate(poly):
            if ci == 0:
                continue
            for d in range(0, n - i + 1):
                if factor[d]:
                    out[i + d] += ci * factor[d]
        poly = out
    return poly


def coeffs_by_recursion(a: Vector, n_max: int) -> List[int]:
    """
    Coefficients A_0, ..., A_{n_max} from the logarithmic-derivative recursion

        A_0 = 1,     n A_n = sum_{i<n} A_i sigma_b(n-i).

    Sieve the divisor data and the twisted divisor sums (O(n log n)), then run the
    convolution (O(n^2)).  All divisions are exact, so everything stays in Z.
    """
    n = n_max
    b = b_vector(a, n)
    sig = [0] * (n + 1)
    for m in range(1, n + 1):
        if b[m] == 0:
            continue
        for j in range(m, n + 1, m):
            sig[j] += m * b[m]
    A = [0] * (n + 1)
    A[0] = 1
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = sum(A[i] * sig[k - i] for i in range(k))
        assert total % k == 0, "recursion must divide exactly"
        A[k] = total // k
    return A


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Arithmetic of the head coefficient
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_pure_head_coeff(c: int) -> bool:
    """A pure (a_2 = 0) head coefficient is characterised by: 8c + 9 is a square."""
    t = 8 * c + 9
    if t < 0:
        return False
    r = isqrt(t)
    return r * r == t


def admissible_vector_with_head(c: int) -> Vector:
    """a_2 = c, a_3 = 2c - 24, a_4 = 24 - 2c: admissible with head coefficient c."""
    return {2: c, 3: 2 * c - 24, 4: 24 - 2 * c}

from __future__ import annotations

from math import comb, gcd, isqrt
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

Vector = Dict[int, int]  # sparse exponent vector a : index k -> a_k (k >= 1)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic data attached to an exponent vector
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def a_of(a: Vector, k: int) -> int:
    """The exponent a_k (zero outside the support)."""
    return a.get(k, 0)


def weight(a: Vector) -> int:
    """The admissibility weight  sum_k k * a_k  (equals 24 for admissible vectors)."""
    return sum(k * v for k, v in a.items())


def b_coeff(a: Vector, m: int) -> int:
    """Divisor data  b_m = sum_{k | m} a_k."""
    return sum(a_of(a, k) for k in range(1, m + 1) if m % k == 0)


def b_vector(a: Vector, n: int) -> List[int]:
    """[b_0 (unused), b_1, ..., b_n], computed by a sieve over multiples: O(n log n)."""
    b = [0] * (n + 1)
    for k, v in a.items():
        if v == 0 or k < 1:
            continue
        for m in range(k, n + 1, k):
            b[m] += v
    return b


def sigma_b(a: Vector, j: int) -> int:
    """Twisted divisor sum  sigma_b(j) = sum_{m | j} m * b_m."""
    return sum(m * b_coeff(a, m) for m in range(1, j + 1) if j % m == 0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Closed forms proved in the paper
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def head_coeff(a: Vector) -> int:
    """c(1) = a_1 (a_1 + 3) / 2 + a_2.  Exact: n(n+3) is always even."""
    a1, a2 = a_of(a, 1), a_of(a, 2)
    return (a1 * (a1 + 3)) // 2 + a2


def constant_coeff(a: Vector) -> int:
    """c(0) = a_1."""
    return a_of(a, 1)


def second_coeff(a: Vector) -> int:
    """c(2) = a_1(a_1+1)(a_1+2)/6 + a_1(a_1 + a_2) + a_1 + a_3."""
    a1, a2, a3 = a_of(a, 1), a_of(a, 2), a_of(a, 3)
    return (a1 * (a1 + 1) * (a1 + 2)) // 6 + a1 * (a1 + a2) + a1 + a3


def head_matrix(a: Vector) -> Tuple[Tuple[int, int, int], ...]:
    """The unipotent 3x3 matrix M(a) = [[1, a_1, c(1)], [0, 1, a_1], [0, 0, 1]]."""
    a1, h = a_of(a, 1), head_coeff(a)
    return ((1, a1, h), (0, 1, a1), (0, 0, 1))


def mat_mul(
    x: Tuple[Tuple[int, int, int], ...], y: Tuple[Tuple[int, int, int], ...]
) -> Tuple[Tuple[int, int, int], ...]:
    """Ordinary 3x3 integer matrix product."""
    return tuple(
        tuple(sum(x[i][k] * y[k][j] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)
    )


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two independent coefficient engines
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def coeffs_by_product(a: Vector, n_max: int, trunc: int | None = None) -> List[int]:
    """
    Coefficients A_0, ..., A_{n_max} of the truncated product
    F^{(N)} = prod_{m=1}^{N} (1 - q^m)^{-b_m}, expanded factor by factor.

    Uses (1-q^m)^{-b} = sum_j C(b+j-1, j) q^{mj} for b >= 0 and the finite
    binomial expansion (1-q^m)^{|b|} for b < 0.  Complexity O(N * n_max) terms.
    """
    n = n_max
    N = n if trunc is None else trunc
    b = b_vector(a, max(N, n))
    poly = [0] * (n + 1)
    poly[0] = 1
    for m in range(1, N + 1):
        e = b[m] if m < len(b) else 0
        if e == 0:
            continue
        # coefficients of (1 - q^m)^{-e} up to degree n, as a list indexed by j
        factor: List[int] = [0] * (n + 1)
        j = 0
        while m * j <= n:
            if e > 0:
                factor[m * j] = comb(e + j - 1, j)
            else:
                factor[m * j] = (-1) ** j * comb(-e, j) if j <= -e else 0
            j += 1
        out = [0] * (n + 1)
        for i, ci in enumerate(poly):
            if ci == 0:
                continue
            for d in range(0, n - i + 1):
                if factor[d]:
                    out[i + d] += ci * factor[d]
        poly = out
    return poly


def coeffs_by_recursion(a: Vector, n_max: int) -> List[int]:
    """
    Coefficients A_0, ..., A_{n_max} from the logarithmic-derivative recursion

        A_0 = 1,     n A_n = sum_{i<n} A_i sigma_b(n-i).

    Sieve the divisor data and the twisted divisor sums (O(n log n)), then run the
    convolution (O(n^2)).  All divisions are exact, so everything stays in Z.
    """
    n = n_max
    b = b_vector(a, n)
    sig = [0] * (n + 1)
    for m in range(1, n + 1):
        if b[m] == 0:
            continue
        for j in range(m, n + 1, m):
            sig[j] += m * b[m]
    A = [0] * (n + 1)
    A[0] = 1
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = sum(A[i] * sig[k - i] for i in range(k))
        assert total % k == 0, "recursion must divide exactly"
        A[k] = total // k
    return A


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Arithmetic of the head coefficient
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_pure_head_coeff(c: int) -> bool:
    """A pure (a_2 = 0) head coefficient is characterised by: 8c + 9 is a square."""
    t = 8 * c + 9
    if t < 0:
        return False
    r = isqrt(t)
    return r * r == t


def admissible_vector_with_head(c: int) -> Vector:
    """a_2 = c, a_3 = 2c - 24, a_4 = 24 - 2c: admissible with head coefficient c."""
    return {2: c, 3: 2 * c - 24, 4: 24 - 2 * c}

def b_vector(a: Vector, n: int) -> List[int]:
    """Divisor data b_m = sum_{k | m} a_k for m = 0..n (index 0 unused)."""
    b = [0] * (n + 1)

            b[m] += v
    return b

    b = b_vector(a, n_max)
    sig = [0] * (n_max + 1)
    for m in range(1, n_max + 1):
        if b[m] == 0:
            continue
        for j in range(m, n_max + 1, m):
            sig[j] += m * b[m]
    A = [0] * (n_max + 1)
    A[0] = 1
    for k in range(1, n_max + 1):
        total = sum(A[i] * sig[k - i] for i in range(k))
        assert total % k == 0
        A[k] = total // k
    return A

    for m in range(1, n + 1):

    return sig

    Method: A_0 = 1 and, for n >= 1,

        n A_n = sum_{i < n} A_i sigma_b(n - i).

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd
from typing import Dict, List, NamedTuple, Optional

Vector = Dict[int, int]


class Certificate(NamedTuple):
    """Outcome of the finite test on the divisor data."""
    divisor_data: List[int]        # b_1 .. b_N
    nonnegative: bool              # b_m >= 0 for all m <= N
    strictly_positive: bool        # additionally b_1 >= 1
    modulus: int                   # d = gcd{b_m : m <= N}
    guarantee: str                 # human-readable conclusion


def divisor_data(a: Vector, n: int) -> List[int]:
    """b_m = sum_{k | m} a_k for m = 1..n (index 0 unused)."""
    b = [0] * (n + 1)
    for k, v in a.items():
        if v == 0 or k < 1:
            continue
        for m in range(k, n + 1, k):
            b[m] += v
    return b


def certify(a: Vector, window: int = 64) -> Certificate:
    """
    Inspect the divisor data b_1..b_window of the exponent vector and emit the
    strongest statement the theory supports:

      * if b_m >= 0 for all m in the window, then A_n >= 0 for all n <= window;
      * if in addition b_1 >= 1, then A_n >= 1 for all n <= window;
      * with d = gcd{b_m}, one has d | n A_n for all n, hence d | A_n whenever
        gcd(d, n) = 1; combining with positivity, A_n >= d on those indices.

    Cost: O(window log window); no power series arithmetic is performed at all.
    """
    b = divisor_data(a, window)[1:]
    nonneg = all(x >= 0 for x in b)
    strict = nonneg and b[0] >= 1
    d = 0
    for x in b:
        d = gcd(d, x)
    parts: List[str] = []
    if strict:
        parts.append("every coefficient A_n is >= 1")
    elif nonneg:
        parts.append("every coefficient A_n is >= 0")
    else:
        parts.append("no positivity guarantee (some b_m is negative)")
    if d > 1:
        parts.append(f"{d} divides A_n for every n coprime to {d}")
        if strict:
            parts.append(f"hence A_n >= {d} for every n coprime to {d}")
    return Certificate(b, nonneg, strict, d, "; ".join(parts))


def verify(a: Vector, window: int = 32) -> bool:
    """
    Numerically confirm the certificate on the window by running the recursion
    n A_n = sum_{i<n} A_i sigma_b(n-i).
    """
    cert = certify(a, window)
    b = divisor_data(a, window)
    sig = [0] * (window + 1)
    for m in range(1, window + 1):
        if b[m]:
            for j in range(m, window + 1, m):
                sig[j] += m * b[m]
    A = [0] * (window + 1)
    A[0] = 1
    for n in range(1, window + 1):
        total = sum(A[i] * sig[n - i] for i in range(n))
        assert total % n == 0
        A[n] = total // n
    if cert.strictly_positive and not all(x >= 1 for x in A):
        return False
    if cert.nonnegative and not all(x >= 0 for x in A):
        return False
    if cert.modulus > 1:
        for n in range(1, window + 1):
            if gcd(cert.modulus, n) == 1 and A[n] % cert.modulus != 0:
                return False
    return True

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, log10
from typing import Dict, List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Vector = Dict[int, int]


def eta_quotient_coefficients(a: Vector, n_max: int) -> List[int]:
    """A_0..A_{n_max} via the twisted-divisor-sum recursion; exact integer arithmetic."""
    b = [0] * (n_max + 1)
    for k, v in a.items():
        if v == 0 or k < 1:
            continue
        for m in range(k, n_max + 1, k):
            b[m] += v
    sig = [0] * (n_max + 1)
    for m in range(1, n_max + 1):
        if b[m]:
            for j in range(m, n_max + 1, m):
                sig[j] += m * b[m]
    A = [0] * (n_max + 1)
    A[0] = 1
    for n in range(1, n_max + 1):
        total = sum(A[i] * sig[n - i] for i in range(n))
        assert total % n == 0
        A[n] = total // n
    return A


def main() -> None:
    n_max = 60
    A = eta_quotient_coefficients({1: 24}, n_max)

    idx = list(range(1, n_max + 1))
    coprime = [n for n in idx if gcd(n, 24) == 1]
    other = [n for n in idx if gcd(n, 24) != 1]

    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
    ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc="lower right")

    colours = ["#c1121f" if gcd(n, 24) == 1 else "#8899bb" for n in idx]
    ax2.bar(idx, residues, color=colours, width=0.75)

    ax2.set_ylabel(r"$A_n$ mod 24")
    ax2.set_title("Residues modulo 24\nred bars (indices coprime to 24) are provably zero")
    ax2.set_yticks(range(0, 25, 4))
    ax2.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.25)

    for n in idx:
        if gcd(n, 24) == 1:
            assert A[n] % 24 == 0, "congruence violated"

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("delta_coefficients.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote delta_coefficients.png")
    print("first coefficients:", A[:8])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

<h1>The Eta Quotient Laboratory</h1>
<p class="sub">
Choose integer exponents \(a_1,\dots,a_6\) for the product
\(\eta_a=\prod_k \eta(k\tau)^{a_k}\). The laboratory computes the divisor data
\(b_m=\sum_{k\mid m}a_k\), the twisted divisor sums
\(\sigma_b(j)=\sum_{m\mid j} m\,b_m\), and every coefficient of
\(q/\eta_a=\prod_m(1-q^m)^{-b_m}=\sum_n A_n q^n\) from the recursion
\(nA_n=\sum_{i<n}A_i\sigma_b(n-i)\) — in exact integer arithmetic — then checks
them against the closed forms for \(c(0)=A_1\), \(c(1)=A_2\) and \(c(2)=A_3\).
</p>

<div class="wrap">

      <h2>Exponent vector</h2>
      <div id="sliders"></div>
      <div class="row" style="margin-top:14px">

        <span id="admis" class="badge"></span>
      </div>

        <button data-v="8,4,0,2,0,0">η<sup>8</sup>η(2τ)<sup>4</sup>η(4τ)<sup>2</sup></button>
        <button data-v="0,1,-22,22,0,0">head coefficient 1</button>
        <button data-v="-1,0,0,0,0,0">η<sup>-1</sup> (partitions)</button>
        <button data-v="1,1,1,0,0,1">ηη(2τ)η(3τ)η(6τ)</button>
      </div>

        Admissibility \(\sum_k k\,a_k=24\) is exactly what makes the leading term of
        \(\eta_a\) equal to \(q\), so that \(1/\eta_a=q^{-1}+c(0)+c(1)q+\cdots\).

<script>
const NMAX = 24, KMAX = 6;
const state = [24,0,0,0,0,0];

function buildSliders(){
  const box = document.getElementById('sliders');
  for(let k=1;k<=KMAX;k++){
    const row = document.createElement('div'); row.className='row';
    row.innerHTML = `<label>a<sub>${k}</sub></label>

  }
  document.querySelectorAll('.presets button').forEach(btn=>{
    btn.addEventListener('click',()=>{
      const vals = btn.dataset.v.split(',').map(Number);
      for(let k=1;k<=KMAX;k++){
        state[k-1]=vals[k-1];
        document.getElementById('s'+k).value=vals[k-1];
        document.getElementById('v'+k).textContent=vals[k-1];
      }
      render();
    });
  });
}

function divisorData(n){
  const b = new Array(n+1).fill(0);
  for(let k=1;k<=KMAX;k++){
    if(state[k-1]===0) continue;
    for(let m=k;m<=n;m+=k) b[m]+=state[k-1];
  }
  return b;
}
function twisted(b,n){
  const s = new Array(n+1).fill(0);
  for(let m=1;m<=n;m++){
    if(b[m]===0) continue;
    const w=m*b[m];
    for(let j=m;j<=n;j+=m) s[j]+=w;
  }
  return s;
}
function coefficients(sig,n){
  const A = new Array(n+1).fill(0n);
  A[0]=1n;
  for(let k=1;k<=n;k++){
    let t=0n;
    for(let i=0;i<k;i++) t += A[i]*BigInt(sig[k-i]);
    A[k] = t / BigInt(k);       // always exact
  }
  return A;
}
function gcd(a,b){a=Math.abs(a);b=Math.abs(b);while(b){[a,b]=[b,a%b];}return a;}

function render(){
  const b = divisorData(NMAX), sig = twisted(b,NMAX), A = coefficients(sig,NMAX);
  const a1=state[0], a2=state[1], a3=state[2];

  // weight / admissibility
  let w=0; for(let k=1;k<=KMAX;k++) w+=k*state[k-1];
  document.getElementById('weight').textContent = w;
  const adm = document.getElementById('admis');
  adm.textContent = (w===24) ? 'admissible' : 'not admissible';
  adm.className = 'badge ' + (w===24?'ok':'no');

  // closed forms
  const c0 = a1;
  const c1 = (a1*(a1+3))/2 + a2;
  const c2 = (a1*(a1+1)*(a1+2))/6 + a1*(a1+a2) + a1 + a3;
  const tick = (x,y)=> (BigInt(x)===y) ? '<span style="color:#5cd6c0">✓ matches recursion</span>'
                                       : '<span style="color:#ff6b6b">mismatch</span>';
  document.getElementById('closed').innerHTML =
    `c(0) = a<sub>1</sub> = <b>${c0}</b>   ${tick(c0,A[1])}<br>`+
    `c(1) = a<sub>1</sub>(a<sub>1</sub>+3)/2 + a<sub>2</sub> = <b>${c1}</b>   ${tick(c1,A[2])}<br>`+
    `c(2) = a<sub>1</sub>(a<sub>1</sub>+1)(a<sub>1</sub>+2)/6 + a<sub>1</sub>(a<sub>1</sub>+a<sub>2</sub>) + a<sub>1</sub> + a<sub>3</sub> = <b>${c2}</b>   ${tick(c2,A[3])}<br>`+
    `<span style="color:#9aa4c8">1/η<sub>a</sub> = q<sup>-1</sup> + ${c0} + ${c1} q + ${c2} q<sup>2</sup> + …</span>`;

  // Heisenberg matrix
  const M = [[1,a1,c1],[0,1,a1],[0,0,1]];
  document.getElementById('mat').innerHTML = M.map((r,i)=>r.map((x,j)=>
     `<span class="${(i===0&&j===2)?'c':''}">${x}</span>`).join('')).join('');

  // divisor data table
  let bt = '<tr><th class="idx">m</th><th>b<sub>m</sub></th><th>σ<sub>b</sub>(m)</th></tr>';
  for(let m=1;m<=12;m++)
    bt += `<tr><td class="idx">${m}</td><td>${b[m]}</td><td>${sig[m]}</td></tr>`;
  document.getElementById('btab').innerHTML = bt;

  let d=0, nonneg=true;
  for(let m=1;m<=NMAX;m++){ d=gcd(d,b[m]); if(b[m]<0) nonneg=false; }
  const strict = nonneg && b[1]>=1;
  document.getElementById('gcdnote').innerHTML =
    `d = gcd{b<sub>m</sub>} = <b>${d}</b>. ` +
    (nonneg ? (strict ? 'All b<sub>m</sub> ≥ 0 and b<sub>1</sub> ≥ 1: every coefficient is guaranteed ≥ 1.'
                      : 'All b<sub>m</sub> ≥ 0: every coefficient is guaranteed ≥ 0.')
            : 'Some b<sub>m</sub> is negative: no positivity guarantee — watch the signs below.') +
    (d>1 ? ` And d = ${d} divides A<sub>n</sub> for every n coprime to ${d}.` : '');

  // coefficients table
  let ct = '<tr><th class="idx">n</th><th>A<sub>n</sub> = c(n−1)</th><th>gcd(n,d)</th><th>d | A<sub>n</sub></th></tr>';
  for(let n=0;n<=NMAX;n++){
    const g = d>0 ? gcd(n,d) : 0;
    const div = d>1 ? (A[n] % BigInt(d) === 0n) : null;
    const hl = (d>1 && n>=1 && g===1);
    ct += `<tr${hl?' style="background:rgba(255,207,92,.09)"':''}>`+
          `<td class="idx${hl?' coprime':''}">${n}</td>`+
          `<td${(A[n]<0n)?' style="color:#ff6b6b"':''}>${A[n].toString()}</td>`+
          `<td>${d>1?g:'-'}</td>`+
          `<td>${div===null?'-':(div?'<span class="divis">yes</span>':'no')}</td></tr>`;
  }
  document.getElementById('ctab').innerHTML = ct;
}

buildSliders();
render();
</script>

<p class="sub">
Eta quotients multiply when exponent vectors add: \(q/\eta_{a+a'}=(q/\eta_a)(q/\eta_{a'})\).
The constant term \(c(0)=a_1\) is therefore additive — but the head coefficient
\(c(1)=a_1(a_1+3)/2+a_2\) is not. Its additivity defect is exactly the bilinear term
\(a_1a_1'\), the cross-term of the degree-two convolution of power series. Move the
sliders and watch the defect appear, and watch the matrices
\(M(a)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&a_1&c(1)\\0&1&a_1\\0&0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\)
multiply exactly as they should in the discrete Heisenberg group.
</p>

### A guided tour: from an infinite product to a non-abelian group law

---

## 0. Where we are going

There is one infinite product that number theory keeps coming back to,

$$\eta(\tau) \;=\; q^{1/24}\prod_{n\ge1}\bigl(1-q^{n}\bigr), \qquad q = e^{2\pi i \tau},$$

the [Dedekind eta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_eta_function). Multiply
finitely many rescaled copies of it together with integer exponents, invert the result,
and look at the very first coefficient that is not forced by normalisation. By the end of
this page you will know that this coefficient equals

$$c(1) \;=\; \frac{a_1(a_1+3)}{2} + a_2,$$

that it obeys a group law belonging to the [Heisenberg group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heisenberg_group)
rather than to $\mathbb{Z}$, and that a single logarithmic derivative gives every
coefficient at once — along with an infinite family of positivity statements and
congruences that no finite computation could reach.

You will also have played with all of it.

---

## 1. Building the object

Fix integers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$, almost all zero, and form the **eta quotient**

$$\eta_a(\tau) \;=\; \prod_{k\ge1}\eta(k\tau)^{a_k}.$$

Negative exponents are allowed. This family contains the modular discriminant
$\Delta = \eta(\tau)^{24}$, the generating function of the
[partition numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_(number_theory)),
and many weight-two newforms of small level.

Each factor contributes $q^{k a_k / 24}$, so the leading power of $q$ is
$q^{\frac{1}{24}\sum_k k a_k}$. There is exactly one normalisation making this a clean
single power of $q$:

$$\boxed{\ \sum_{k\ge1} k\, a_k \;=\; 24\ }$$

Call such a vector **admissible** — the same $24$ that appears in $\eta^{24} = \Delta$,
in the [Leech lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leech_lattice), and in the $1/24$
inside $\eta$ itself.

<details>
<summary><b>Why admissibility gives the clean product form (click to expand)</b></summary>

Under $\sum_k k a_k = 24$ the fractional powers cancel and

$$\eta_a(\tau) \;=\; q\prod_{m\ge1}\bigl(1-q^m\bigr)^{b_m}, \qquad b_m \;=\; \sum_{k\mid m}a_k .$$

The exponent $b_m$ is a **divisor sum** of the original exponents: the factor
$\eta(k\tau)$ contributes $(1-q^{kn})$ for every $n \ge 1$, so the term $q^m$ collects a
contribution from every divisor $k$ of $m$. This regrouping — invertible by
[Möbius inversion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius_inversion_formula) — is why
the arithmetic of eta quotients is really the arithmetic of divisor functions. Keep an
eye on it: for $\Delta$ the exponent vector is supported at a single index, yet the
divisor data are the *constant* sequence $b_m = 24$.
</details>

Inverting and clearing the pole gives the object of study:

$$F_a(q) \;=\; \frac{q}{\eta_a} \;=\; \prod_{m\ge1}\bigl(1-q^m\bigr)^{-b_m} \;=\; \sum_{n\ge0}A_n q^n,
\qquad \frac{1}{\eta_a} \;=\; q^{-1} + c(0) + c(1)q + \cdots$$

with $A_n = c(n-1)$. This shape — a $q$-expansion beginning $q^{-1}$ — is the normal form
of a [Hauptmodul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hauptmodul), the shape in which the
McKay–Thompson series of [monstrous moonshine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monstrous_moonshine)
are written. The coefficient $c(1)$ is the first genuinely free invariant.

## 3. The head coefficient, and how one proves it

> **Head Coefficient Theorem.** For every finitely supported exponent vector $a$,
> $$c(1) \;=\; \frac{a_1(a_1+3)}{2} + a_2,$$
> and the earlier coefficients are $c(-1) = 1$ and $c(0) = a_1$.

Two things are surprising. Only $a_1$ and $a_2$ appear — the exponents of
$\eta(3\tau), \eta(4\tau),\dots$ are invisible in this degree because their factors start
at $q^3$. And the dependence on $a_1$ is *quadratic*, even though eta quotients multiply
when exponent vectors add.

<details>
<summary><b>The two-jet proof in full (click to reveal)</b></summary>

Write $J(f) = (c_1, c_2)$ when $f = 1 + c_1q + c_2q^2 + O(q^3)$. Convolution gives the
group law

$$J(fg) \;=\; \bigl(c_1+d_1,\ c_2 + c_1d_1 + d_2\bigr),$$

inversion gives $J(u^{-1}) = (-c_1,\ c_1^2 - c_2)$, and an induction in both directions
from $n = 0$ gives the power law

$$J(u^n) \;=\; \Bigl(n c_1,\ n c_2 + \binom{n}{2}c_1^2\Bigr), \qquad n \in \mathbb{Z}.$$

That binomial coefficient is the degree-two truncation of $\exp(n \log u)$, and it is the
entire source of the quadratic term.

Now the basic factors: $J(1-q) = (-1, 0)$, $J(1-q^2) = (0,-1)$, and $J(1-q^m) = (0,0)$ for
$m \ge 3$. With $b_1 = a_1$ and $b_2 = a_1 + a_2$,

$$J\bigl((1-q)^{-b_1}\bigr) = \Bigl(a_1,\ \tfrac{a_1(a_1+1)}{2}\Bigr), \qquad
J\bigl((1-q^2)^{-b_2}\bigr) = (0,\ a_1+a_2),$$

and multiplying,

$$c(1) \;=\; \frac{a_1(a_1+1)}{2} + a_1 + a_2 \;=\; \frac{a_1(a_1+3)}{2} + a_2 .$$

Every further factor has jet $(0,0)$, so it changes nothing — which is also the reason the
answer does not depend on how far the product is truncated. $\blacksquare$
</details>

Sanity check: $\Delta = \eta^{24}$ has $a_1 = 24$, so $c(1) = 24 \cdot 27 / 2 = 324$, and
indeed $1/\Delta = q^{-1} + 24 + 324q + 3200q^2 + 25650q^3 + \cdots$.

One degree deeper, the [tetrahedral numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahedral_number)
$\binom{n}{3}$ take over from the triangular ones and give

$$c(2) \;=\; \frac{a_1(a_1+1)(a_1+2)}{6} + a_1(a_1+a_2) + a_1 + a_3,$$

which for $a_1 = 24$ returns $2600 + 576 + 24 = 3200$, as it must.

## 4. Why the answer is quadratic: a group law in disguise

Exponent vectors add, eta quotients multiply: $F_{a+a'} = F_a F_{a'}$. So one might hope
every natural invariant were additive. The constant term is: $c(0) = a_1$. The head
coefficient is not.

> **The Heisenberg Cocycle.**
> $$c(1)(a + a') \;=\; c(1)(a) + c(1)(a') + a_1a_1'.$$

The defect is a symmetric bilinear form — and it is not sloppiness, it is the cross-term
$c_1d_1$ in the jet group law above. A cocycle of that shape has a name: package the pair
into

$$M(a) \;=\; \begin{pmatrix}1 & a_1 & c(1)\\ 0&1&a_1\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad
M(a+a') \;=\; M(a)\,M(a'), \qquad \det M(a) = 1 .$$

This is a homomorphism into the **discrete Heisenberg group**: the smallest non-abelian
nilpotent group, the one behind the
[canonical commutation relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_commutation_relation).
The head coefficient lives in its centre.

## 5. Every degree at once: the logarithmic derivative

Jet calculus does not scale — degree four would need a whole new formalism. The uniform
statement comes from the [Euler operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_operator)
$\theta = q\,\frac{d}{dq}$. Since $\theta\log$ turns products into sums, and
$\theta \log (1-q^m) = -m\,\frac{q^m}{1-q^m}$,

$$\theta \log F_a \;=\; \sum_{m\ge1} m\,b_m \frac{q^m}{1-q^m} \;=\; \sum_{j\ge1}\sigma_b(j)\,q^j,
\qquad \sigma_b(j) \;=\; \sum_{m\mid j} m\,b_m .$$

The structure constants $\sigma_b(j)$ are **twisted divisor sums** — a weighted version of
the classical $\sigma_1$; for $q/\Delta$ they are just $24\,\sigma_1(j)$.

> **Recursion Theorem.** $A_0 = 1$ and, for every $n \ge 1$,
> $$n\,A_n \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} A_i\,\sigma_b(n-i).$$

<details>
<summary><b>The one-line proof (click to reveal)</b></summary>

Multiply the definition of the logarithmic derivative by $F$ to get
$F\cdot\theta\log F = \theta F$, and take the coefficient of $q^n$. The right-hand side is
$nA_n$. The left-hand side is $\sum_{i\le n} A_i\,\sigma_b(n-i)$, whose $i = n$ term
vanishes because $\theta\log F$ has no constant term. $\blacksquare$
</details>

Crucially, $\sigma_b$ is **additive** in the exponent vector — unlike the head
coefficient. That is the punchline of the whole theory: the logarithm side is exactly
linear, and all the non-linearity of the coefficients is the non-linearity of $\exp$.
Unipotent groups are truncations of $\exp$; that is why they govern the tower.

## 6. Two theorems no finite computation can see

Because the recursion holds in every degree, sign and divisibility information flows from
the divisor data to *all* the coefficients at once.

> **Positivity.** If $b_m \ge 0$ for every $m$, then $A_n \ge 0$ for every $n$. If
> moreover $b_1 \ge 1$, then $A_n \ge 1$ for every $n$.

> **Congruence.** If $d$ divides every $b_m$, then $d \mid n A_n$ for every $n \ge 1$;
> and if $\gcd(d,n) = 1$, then $d \mid A_n$.

<details>
<summary><b>Both proofs, in four lines (click to reveal)</b></summary>

If every $b_m \ge 0$ then every $\sigma_b(j) \ge 0$, and $nA_n$ is a sum of products of
nonnegatives — induct. If moreover $b_1 \ge 1$, then since $m = 1$ divides every $j$ we
get $\sigma_b(j) \ge b_1 \ge 1$, so each of the $n$ summands is at least $1$, giving
$nA_n \ge n$.

If $d \mid b_m$ for all $m$ then $d \mid \sigma_b(j)$ for all $j$, so $d \mid nA_n$;
coprimality of $d$ and $n$ lets you cancel. $\blacksquare$
</details>

For $q/\Delta$, where $b_m = 24$ for every $m$, both hypotheses hold: the sequence
$1, 24, 324, 3200, 25650, 176256, \dots$ is positive throughout, and $24 \mid A_n$ whenever
$\gcd(n, 24) = 1$. Combining the two gives $A_n \ge 24$ on those indices with no
computation at all.

And the coprimality is essential: $A_2 = 324$, $A_3 = 3200$, $A_4 = 25650$ are *not*
divisible by $24$. The picture below shows both halves of the phenomenon on the first

## 7. Which numbers can be head coefficients?

Restrict to *pure* powers $\eta(\tau)^{a_1}$, so $a_2 = 0$ and $c(1) = a_1(a_1+3)/2$.
Completing the square gives $8c(1) + 9 = (2a_1+3)^2$, hence:

> **Diophantine Characterisation.** An integer $c$ is the head coefficient of a pure eta
> power if and only if $8c + 9$ is a perfect square.

So $c = 1$ is *unattainable* — $17$ is not a square. Two exponents give the same value
exactly under the reflection $a_1 \mapsto -3-a_1$. And although the real parabola dips to
$-9/8$, the integers cannot: $c \ge -1$ always, attained exactly at $a_1 = -1$ and
$a_1 = -2$. A small, sharp instance of integrality rigidity.

{{visualization:0}}

Let $a_2$ back in, though, and every obstruction dissolves — $a_2$ enters the formula
linearly, so it is a free dial:

> **Surjectivity.** Every integer $c$ is the head coefficient of an *admissible* exponent
> vector: take $a_2 = c$, $a_3 = 2c-24$, $a_4 = 24-2c$, whose weight is
> $2c + 6c - 72 + 96 - 8c = 24$.

Thus $c = 1$, impossible for a pure power, is realised by $\eta(2\tau)\,\eta(3\tau)^{-22}\,\eta(4\tau)^{22}$.

## 8. The tropical shadow, and what it forgets

Any power series has an **order**: the index of its first non-zero coefficient. Order is a
[valuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valuation_(algebra)) — it adds under
multiplication and behaves like a minimum under addition — which is precisely the
arithmetic of the [tropical semiring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_semiring),
where $\otimes$ is ordinary addition and $\oplus$ is $\min$. Transporting the order there
gives a genuine multiplicative map $T$ with $T(fg) = T(f)\otimes T(g)$ and
$T(f)\oplus T(g) \le T(f+g)$.

Applied to our family the result is comically degenerate: $F_a$ has constant term $1$, so
its order is $0$ and $T(F_a)$ is the tropical unit for *every* $a$. The normalisation
pushed all valuation-theoretic information into the explicit factor $q$ we divided out.

That degeneracy is the point. The tropical layer is *strictly coarser* than the head
coefficient: $\Delta$ and the trivial quotient have identical tropical shadows and head
coefficients differing by $324$. The invariant tower has a bottom floor that is tropical,
additive and blind — and a first floor that is Heisenberg, non-abelian and sharp.

## 10. What to take away

Start with an infinite product built from a handful of integers. Normalise so the leading
term is $q$. Invert. The first free coefficient is $a_1(a_1+3)/2 + a_2$ — and quadratics
in this business always mean a cocycle, and a cocycle always means a group. Here the group
is the Heisenberg group.

One degree deeper, tetrahedral numbers appear and a unipotent tower comes into view:
linear, then quadratic, then cubic, each layer a new commutator. Behind all of it sits a
single recursion whose structure constants are twisted divisor sums, honestly linear in
the input. And from that one recursion: every coefficient of $1/\Delta$ is positive, and
every coefficient indexed by a number coprime to $24$ is divisible by $24$ — two infinite
families of facts, invisible to any finite calculation, both consequences of the same line
of algebra.

      have h1 : Jet (f i) 0 0 := h i (by simp)
      have h2 : Jet (∏ j ∈ s, f j) 0 0 := ih fun j hj => h j (by simp [hj])

  have h1 : n * (0 : ℤ) = 0 := by ring

  have h2 : (0 : ℤ) + 0 * c1 + c2 = c2 := by ring

  have h := hf.mul hg
  have h1 : c1 + (0 : ℤ) = c1 := by ring
  have h2 : c2 + c1 * (0 : ℤ) + 0 = c2 := by ring
  rw [h1, h2] at h
  exact h

open PowerSeries Finset

/-! ## The logarithmic derivative on units of `ℤ⟦X⟧` -/

/-- The logarithmic derivative `logD u = X · u' · u⁻¹` of a unit of `ℤ⟦X⟧`.
The factor `X` makes it the *Euler operator* `q d/dq`, which is what turns
products of `(1 - q^m)` into divisor sums. -/
noncomputable def logD (u : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ :=
  X * (d⁄dX ℤ) (u : PowerSeries ℤ) * ((u⁻¹ : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ)

lemma val_mul_logD (u : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) :
    (u : PowerSeries ℤ) * logD u = X * (d⁄dX ℤ) (u : PowerSeries ℤ) := by
  have h : (u : PowerSeries ℤ) * ((u⁻¹ : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) = 1 := u.mul_inv
  unfold logD
  linear_combination (X * (d⁄dX ℤ) (u : PowerSeries ℤ)) * h

@[simp] lemma logD_one : logD 1 = 0 := by
  simp [logD]

/-- `logD` turns the multiplicative group of units of `ℤ⟦X⟧` into an additive group. -/
lemma logD_mul (u v : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : logD (u * v) = logD u + logD v := by
  have hu : (u : PowerSeries ℤ) * ((u⁻¹ : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) = 1 := u.mul_inv
  have hv : (v : PowerSeries ℤ) * ((v⁻¹ : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) = 1 := v.mul_inv
  have hleib : (d⁄dX ℤ) ((u : PowerSeries ℤ) * (v : PowerSeries ℤ))
      = (u : PowerSeries ℤ) * (d⁄dX ℤ) (v : PowerSeries ℤ)
        + (v : PowerSeries ℤ) * (d⁄dX ℤ) (u : PowerSeries ℤ) := by
    simp
  unfold logD
  rw [mul_inv_rev, Units.val_mul, Units.val_mul, hleib]
  linear_combination
    (X * (d⁄dX ℤ) (v : PowerSeries ℤ) * ((v⁻¹ : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ)) * hu
      + (X * (d⁄dX ℤ) (u : PowerSeries ℤ) * ((u⁻¹ : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ)) * hv

lemma logD_inv (u : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : logD u⁻¹ = - logD u := by
  have h := logD_mul u u⁻¹
  rw [mul_inv_cancel, logD_one] at h
  linear_combination -h

  induction n using Int.induction_on with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih => rw [zpow_add_one, logD_mul, ih]; module
  | pred k ih => rw [zpow_sub_one, logD_mul, logD_inv, ih]; module

lemma logD_prod {ι : Type*} [DecidableEq ι] (s : Finset ι) (f : ι → (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) :
    logD (∏ i ∈ s, f i) = ∑ i ∈ s, logD (f i) := by
  induction s using Finset.induction with
  | empty => simp
  | insert i s hi ih => rw [Finset.prod_insert hi, Finset.sum_insert hi, logD_mul, ih]

noncomputable def geomSeries (m : ℕ) : PowerSeries ℤ :=

def sigmaB (a : ℕ → ℤ) (N j : ℕ) : ℤ :=
  ∑ m ∈ (Icc 1 N).filter (fun m => m ∣ j), (m : ℤ) * bCoeff a m

/-- Unlike the head coefficient (which satisfies a Heisenberg cocycle rule),

theorem sigmaB_add (a a' : ℕ → ℤ) (N j : ℕ) :

    unfold bCoeff
    rw [← Finset.sum_add_distrib]

  rw [hb]; ring

  rw [logD_etaQuotientProd, map_sum, sigmaB, Finset.sum_filter]
  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl fun m hm => ?_
  have hm1 : 1 ≤ m := (Finset.mem_Icc.mp hm).1

  by_cases hd : m ∣ j
  · have hle : m ≤ j := Nat.le_of_dvd (by omega) hd
    rw [if_pos ⟨hd, hle⟩, if_pos hd]
    ring
  · rw [if_neg (by tauto), if_neg hd]
    ring

@[simp] lemma coeff_zero_logD_etaQuotientProd (a : ℕ → ℤ) (N : ℕ) :

  refine Finset.sum_eq_zero fun m hm => ?_

    if_neg (show ¬ (m ∣ 0 ∧ m ≤ 0) from fun h => by omega)]

/-! ## The main recursion -/

/-- **Main theorem (all degrees).**  Writing `F = ∏_{m=1}^{N} (1 - X^m)^{-b m}` for the
normalised eta quotient, its coefficients satisfy, for every `n ≥ 1`,

  `n · [q^n] F = ∑_{i < n} [q^i] F · σ_b(n - i)`,

where `σ_b(j) = ∑_{m ∣ j, m ≤ N} m · b m`.  Together with `[q^0] F = 1` this
determines *every* coefficient of the eta quotient from the divisor data `b`. -/
theorem coeff_recursion (a : ℕ → ℤ) (N : ℕ) {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    (n : ℤ) * coeff n ((etaQuotientProd a N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ)

          coeff i ((etaQuotientProd a N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ)
            * sigmaB a N (n - i) := by
  set F : PowerSeries ℤ := ((etaQuotientProd a N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) with hF
  set L : PowerSeries ℤ := logD (etaQuotientProd a N) with hL
  have hkey : F * L = X * (d⁄dX ℤ) F := val_mul_logD _
  obtain ⟨n', rfl⟩ : ∃ n', n = n' + 1 := ⟨n - 1, by omega⟩
  have hlhs : coeff (n' + 1) (X * (d⁄dX ℤ) F) = ((n' : ℤ) + 1) * coeff (n' + 1) F := by
    rw [PowerSeries.coeff_succ_X_mul, PowerSeries.coeff_derivative]
    ring
  have hrhs : coeff (n' + 1) (F * L)
      = ∑ i ∈ range (n' + 1), coeff i F * sigmaB a N (n' + 1 - i) := by
    rw [PowerSeries.coeff_mul, Finset.Nat.sum_antidiagonal_eq_sum_range_succ_mk,
      Finset.sum_range_succ]
    have hlast : coeff (n' + 1) F * coeff (n' + 1 - (n' + 1)) L = 0 := by
      rw [show n' + 1 - (n' + 1) = 0 by omega, coeff_zero_eq_constantCoeff_apply, hL,
        coeff_zero_logD_etaQuotientProd]
      ring
    rw [hlast, add_zero]
    refine Finset.sum_congr rfl fun i hi => ?_
    have hi' : i < n' + 1 := Finset.mem_range.mp hi
    rw [hL, coeff_logD_etaQuotientProd a N (show 1 ≤ n' + 1 - i by omega)]
  rw [← hkey] at hlhs
  rw [hrhs] at hlhs
  push_cast
  linarith [hlhs]

/-! ## Cross-checks: re-deriving the head coefficients -/

/-- The normalisation `[q^0] F = 1`, proved directly from the fact that `constantCoeff`
is a ring homomorphism (so induces a group homomorphism on units), without any input
from the jet calculus of `Tropical.EtaQuotientHeadCoeff`.  It also holds for every
truncation `N`, with no lower bound. -/
theorem constantCoeff_etaQuotientProd_direct (a : ℕ → ℤ) (N : ℕ) :
    constantCoeff ((etaQuotientProd a N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) = 1 := by
  set φ : PowerSeries ℤ →* ℤ := (constantCoeff : PowerSeries ℤ →+* ℤ).toMonoidHom with hφ
  have key : Units.map φ (etaQuotientProd a N) = 1 := by
    rw [etaQuotientProd, map_prod]
    refine Finset.prod_eq_one fun m hm => ?_
    have hm1 : 1 ≤ m := (Finset.mem_Icc.mp hm).1
    have hc : Units.map φ (oneSubXPow m) = 1 := by
      refine Units.ext ?_
      rw [Units.coe_map, Units.val_one, hφ]
      show constantCoeff ((oneSubXPow m : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) = 1
      rw [coe_oneSubXPow hm1, ← coeff_zero_eq_constantCoeff_apply, coeff_one_sub_X_pow,
        if_pos rfl, if_neg (show ¬ ((0:ℕ) = m) by omega)]
      ring
    rw [map_zpow, hc, one_zpow]
  have hval := congrArg Units.val key
  rw [Units.coe_map, Units.val_one, hφ] at hval
  exact hval

/-- `c(0) = a₁`, re-derived from the recursion (independently of the jet calculus). -/
theorem coeff_one_via_recursion (a : ℕ → ℤ) {N : ℕ} (hN : 1 ≤ N) :
    coeff 1 ((etaQuotientProd a N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) = a 1 := by
  have h := coeff_recursion a N (n := 1) (by omega)
  rw [Finset.sum_range_one, coeff_zero_eq_constantCoeff_apply,
    constantCoeff_etaQuotientProd_direct a N] at h
  rw [show (1:ℕ) - 0 = 1 from rfl, sigmaB_one a hN] at h
  push_cast at h
  linarith [h]

/-- **The head coefficient, re-derived.**  `c(1) = a₁(a₁+3)/2 + a₂`, obtained from the
logarithmic-derivative recursion.  This proof shares no lemma with the `2`-jet
computation of `coeff_two_etaQuotientProd`, so the two together form an independent
double check of the head-coefficient formula. -/
theorem coeff_two_via_recursion (a : ℕ → ℤ) {N : ℕ} (hN : 2 ≤ N) :
    coeff 2 ((etaQuotientProd a N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) = headCoeff a := by
  have h := coeff_recursion a N (n := 2) (by omega)
  rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, Finset.sum_range_one] at h
  rw [show (2:ℕ) - 0 = 2 from rfl, show (2:ℕ) - 1 = 1 from rfl] at h
  rw [coeff_zero_eq_constantCoeff_apply, constantCoeff_etaQuotientProd_direct a N,
    sigmaB_one a (by omega), sigmaB_two a hN, coeff_one_via_recursion a (by omega)] at h
  push_cast at h
  have hh : (2:ℤ) * coeff 2 ((etaQuotientProd a N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ)
      = 2 * headCoeff a := by
    rw [two_mul_headCoeff]
    linear_combination h
  linarith [hh]

/-- The classical value `c(1) = 324` for `1/Δ = q^{-1} + 24 + 324 q + ⋯`, obtained
from the recursion. -/
theorem coeff_two_delta_via_recursion {N : ℕ} (hN : 2 ≤ N) :
    coeff 2 ((etaQuotientProd (fun k => if k = 1 then 24 else 0) N :
      (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) = 324 := by
  rw [coeff_two_via_recursion _ hN]
  norm_num [headCoeff]

/-! ## Stability of the twisted divisor sums -/

/-- For `N ≥ j` the truncation is invisible: `σ_b(j)` is the full divisor sum. -/
theorem sigmaB_eq_divisors (a : ℕ → ℤ) {N j : ℕ} (hj : 1 ≤ j) (hN : j ≤ N) :
    sigmaB a N j = ∑ m ∈ j.divisors, (m : ℤ) * bCoeff a m := by
  unfold sigmaB
  refine Finset.sum_congr ?_ fun _ _ => rfl
  ext m
  simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_Icc, Nat.mem_divisors]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨_, hd⟩; exact ⟨hd, by omega⟩
  · rintro ⟨hd, _⟩
    have hm1 : 1 ≤ m := Nat.one_le_iff_ne_zero.mpr (by rintro rfl; omega)
    exact ⟨⟨hm1, le_trans (Nat.le_of_dvd (by omega) hd) hN⟩, hd⟩

/-- Consequently the recursion — hence every coefficient — is independent of the
truncation `N` as soon as `N ≥ n`. -/
theorem sigmaB_stable (a : ℕ → ℤ) {N N' j : ℕ} (hj : 1 ≤ j) (hN : j ≤ N) (hN' : j ≤ N') :
    sigmaB a N j = sigmaB a N' j := by
  rw [sigmaB_eq_divisors a hj hN, sigmaB_eq_divisors a hj hN']

/-!
# Divisibility congruences for eta-quotient coefficients

The recursion `n · c(n) = ∑_{i<n} c(i) · σ_b(n-i)` of `Tropical.EtaQuotientRecursion`
has an immediate arithmetic consequence that no finite jet computation can see: every
common divisor `d` of the divisor data `b` divides each structure constant `σ_b(j)`,
hence divides `n · c(n)` for every `n ≥ 1`.  Whenever `d` is coprime to `n` this
forces `d ∣ c(n)`.

For `1/Δ`, where `b m = 24` for every `m ≥ 1`, this gives

  `24 ∣ c(n)`  for every `n ≥ 1` coprime to `24`

(`coeff_delta_dvd_of_coprime`), and in general `24 ∣ n · c(n)`.  The numerical data
`c(1) = 24`, `c(2) = 324`, `c(3) = 3200`, `c(4) = 25650`, `c(5) = 176256` show the
coprimality hypothesis is not removable: `324`, `3200`, `25650` are *not* divisible by
`24`, while `24` and `176256 = 24 · 7344` are.  This is verified in Lean below by
`coeff_two_delta_not_dvd_24`.
-/

namespace EtaHead

open PowerSeries Finset

/-! ## Divisibility of the structure constants -/

/-- A common divisor of the divisor data `b` divides every twisted divisor sum. -/
theorem dvd_sigmaB {d : ℤ} (a : ℕ → ℤ) (N j : ℕ)
    (hd : ∀ m, 1 ≤ m → m ≤ N → d ∣ bCoeff a m) : d ∣ sigmaB a N j := by
  unfold sigmaB
  refine Finset.dvd_sum fun m hm => ?_
  obtain ⟨hmIcc, _⟩ := Finset.mem_filter.mp hm
  obtain ⟨hm1, hmN⟩ := Finset.mem_Icc.mp hmIcc
  exact Dvd.dvd.mul_left (hd m hm1 hmN) _

/-- **Congruence from the recursion.**  If `d` divides every `b m` (`1 ≤ m ≤ N`) then
`d ∣ n · c(n)` for every `n ≥ 1`. -/
theorem dvd_nat_mul_coeff {d : ℤ} (a : ℕ → ℤ) {N : ℕ} {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n)
    (hd : ∀ m, 1 ≤ m → m ≤ N → d ∣ bCoeff a m) :
    d ∣ (n : ℤ) * coeff n ((etaQuotientProd a N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) := by
  rw [coeff_recursion a N hn]
  refine Finset.dvd_sum fun i _ => ?_
  exact Dvd.dvd.mul_left (dvd_sigmaB a N _ hd) _

/-- If moreover `d` is coprime to `n`, the divisibility descends to `c(n)` itself. -/
theorem dvd_coeff_of_isCoprime {d : ℤ} (a : ℕ → ℤ) {N : ℕ} {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n)
    (hd : ∀ m, 1 ≤ m → m ≤ N → d ∣ bCoeff a m) (hcop : IsCoprime d (n : ℤ)) :
    d ∣ coeff n ((etaQuotientProd a N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) :=
  hcop.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left (dvd_nat_mul_coeff a hn hd)

/-! ## The case of `1/Δ` -/

/-- `24 ∣ n · c(n)` for the coefficients of `q/Δ`. -/
theorem dvd_24_nat_mul_coeff_delta {N n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    (24 : ℤ) ∣ (n : ℤ) * coeff n
      ((etaQuotientProd deltaExp N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) := by
  refine dvd_nat_mul_coeff deltaExp hn (fun m hm1 _ => ?_)
  rw [bCoeff_deltaExp hm1]

/-- **A moonshine-flavoured congruence.**  For every `n ≥ 1` coprime to `24`, the
`n`-th coefficient of `q/Δ` is divisible by `24`. -/
theorem coeff_delta_dvd_of_coprime {N n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) (hcop : Nat.gcd n 24 = 1) :
    (24 : ℤ) ∣ coeff n ((etaQuotientProd deltaExp N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) := by
  refine dvd_coeff_of_isCoprime deltaExp hn (fun m hm1 _ => by rw [bCoeff_deltaExp hm1]) ?_
  rw [Int.isCoprime_iff_gcd_eq_one]
  simpa [Int.gcd, Nat.gcd_comm] using hcop

/-- The coprimality hypothesis in `coeff_delta_dvd_of_coprime` cannot be dropped: for
`n = 2` the coefficient is `324`, and `24 ∤ 324`. -/
theorem coeff_two_delta_not_dvd_24 {N : ℕ} (hN : 2 ≤ N) :
    ¬ ((24 : ℤ) ∣ coeff 2
      ((etaQuotientProd deltaExp N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ)) := by
  rw [coeff_two_delta hN]
  decide

/-- The first instance of the congruence: the `q`-coefficient `24` is divisible by
`24`. -/
theorem coeff_one_delta_dvd_24 (N : ℕ) :
    (24 : ℤ) ∣ coeff 1 ((etaQuotientProd deltaExp N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) :=
  coeff_delta_dvd_of_coprime (by omega) (by decide)

/-! ## A general two-sided statement -/

/-- Combining positivity with the congruence: for `1/Δ` and `n ≥ 1` coprime to `24`,
the coefficient `c(n-1)` is a *positive* multiple of `24`, hence at least `24`. -/
theorem coeff_delta_ge_24_of_coprime {N n : ℕ} (hN : 1 ≤ N) (hn : 1 ≤ n)
    (hcop : Nat.gcd n 24 = 1) :
    24 ≤ coeff n ((etaQuotientProd deltaExp N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) := by
  obtain ⟨t, ht⟩ := coeff_delta_dvd_of_coprime (N := N) hn hcop
  have hpos : 1 ≤ coeff n ((etaQuotientProd deltaExp N : (PowerSeries ℤ)ˣ) : PowerSeries ℤ) :=
    coeff_delta_pos hN n
  have ht1 : 1 ≤ t := by nlinarith [ht, hpos]
  nlinarith [ht, ht1]

end EtaHead",
